01.event: The Sages urged him to marry and have children, and he deflected by saying that had he merited it he would already have had children from his first wife.
01.turn: The Gemara says his reply was only an excuse; the real reason was that he had become impotent from Rav Huna's lengthy discourses.
01.summary: The Sages told Rabbi Abba bar Zavda to marry and father children. He answered that if he had merited it he would already have had children by his first wife. The Gemara explains that this was a brush-off: he had really been made impotent by sitting through Rav Huna's sermons.
01.missing: It is a brief exchange cited to settle a legal point; it has no real ending and nothing is said of what he did next.

02.event: Rabbi Yohanan expounded a law of notar, and Rabbi Elazar raised an objection from a baraita on the verse 'and on the day'.
02.turn: Rabbi Elazar's baraita and its parallel proof left Rabbi Yohanan silent; afterward Reish Lakish told Rabbi Yohanan that Elazar's teaching was a baraita from Torat Kohanim, not his own.
02.outcome: Rabbi Yohanan went out, learned all of Torat Kohanim in three days and mastered it in three months.
02.summary: Rabbi Yohanan was sitting and teaching a law of notar when Rabbi Elazar challenged him with a baraita, and Yohanan had no reply. After Elazar left, Yohanan praised him to Reish Lakish as teaching like Moses from the Almighty. Reish Lakish said it was only a baraita in Torat Kohanim, so Yohanan went off and learned the whole work in three days and understood it in three months.

03.actor: The daughters-in-law of Abdan, and the two Sages sent by Rabbi
03.event: Abdan's daughters-in-law rebelled against their husbands, and Rabbi sent a pair of Sages to examine them.
03.turn: When women told them the husbands were coming, the daughters-in-law answered 'Let them be your husbands', rejecting their marriages.
03.outcome: Rabbi said there is no greater refusal than this, and the Gemara concludes that they must have been merely betrothed.
03.summary: Abdan's daughters-in-law rebelled against their husbands, so Rabbi sent two Sages to look into it. Other women told the daughters-in-law that their husbands were arriving, and they replied 'Let them be your husbands.' Rabbi declared that there is no greater refusal than this.
03.missing: What happened to the marriages afterward is not told; the passage only uses the incident as evidence for the law of refusal.

04.event: Others confronted Ben Azzai for expounding the duty to procreate well while not fulfilling it himself.
04.turn: He answered that his soul yearned for Torah and the world can be maintained by others.
04.summary: Ben Azzai's colleagues pointed out that he preached the commandment to be fruitful and multiply beautifully but did not practice it. He replied that his soul was devoted to Torah and that the world can be kept going by others.
04.missing: It is a single rebuke and reply with no setting and no further consequence.

05.event: Passed over for head of the yeshiva, Ilfa hung himself from a ship's mast and vowed to drown unless he could trace any baraita he was told back to a mishna.
05.turn: An old man came and taught him a baraita on a dying man's instruction to give his sons a shekel, and asked where it appears in the Mishna.
05.outcome: Ilfa asked whose opinion it was and answered that it is Rabbi Meir, who holds it a mitzva to fulfill the words of the dead, and so he passed the test.
05.summary: When Rabbi Yohanan was appointed head of the yeshiva instead of Ilfa, Ilfa suspended himself from a ship's mast and swore he would fall and drown if someone brought him a baraita he could not ground in a mishna. An old man came and taught him a baraita about a shekel for a dying man's sons. Ilfa asked whose opinion it was and then identified it as Rabbi Meir's, so he answered the challenge.

06.actor: A man sent by his father
06.event: A father told his son to climb up a building and fetch chicks, and the son dispatched the mother bird and took the young.
06.turn: On his way back down he fell and died despite having kept both mitzvot.
06.outcome: The Gemara concludes that the promised good and long days must refer to the world to come, not this one.
06.summary: A man's father told him to climb up to the roof and bring him chicks. He climbed, sent away the mother bird as the law requires, and took the young, thus honoring his father and keeping the mitzva. Coming back down he fell and died, which is cited to show the rewards promised in the verses belong to the world that is entirely good and long.

09.actor: A man who betrothed a minor girl, and Ravina
09.event: A man betrothed a minor girl with a bundle of vegetables in the marketplace without her father's consent.
09.turn: Ravina ruled that even the view that we suspect the father consented applies only to a dignified betrothal, not a degrading one.
09.outcome: The betrothal was treated as not raising the concern, because it was degrading.
09.summary: A man betrothed a minor girl with a bundle of vegetables in the marketplace. Ravina ruled that we do not suspect her father wanted this betrothal, since it was done in a degrading way.
09.missing: It is a bare case report followed by a ruling; nothing is said about the people or what became of them.

10.actor: A man testifying before Reish Lakish, and Rabbi Elazar
10.event: A man told Reish Lakish that another man had established himself as a priest because he read first in the synagogue.
10.turn: Reish Lakish asked whether he had seen him take a share of terumah at the threshing floor, and Rabbi Elazar objected that priesthood does not cease where there is no threshing floor.
10.outcome: On a later occasion Reish Lakish realized Elazar was repeating Rabbi Yohanan's ruling and rebuked him for not saying so.
10.summary: A man came before Reish Lakish claiming another was a priest because he had been called to read first in the synagogue. Reish Lakish demanded to know whether he had seen him get terumah at the threshing floor, and Rabbi Elazar protested that there might be no threshing floor. Later, when Rabbi Yohanan said the same thing, Reish Lakish glared at Elazar for not saying it was Yohanan's ruling.
10.missing: The first case's outcome is not stated, and the sequel is in the following context segment rather than the passage.

11.actor: Rav Shimi bar Hiyya and Rav
11.event: A man betrothed a woman with a bundle of rags, and Rav Shimi sat before Rav and appraised whether it was worth a peruta.
11.turn: The Gemara notes that if it was not worth a peruta she would not be betrothed, which seems to contradict Shmuel, and resolves it as certain versus uncertain betrothal.
11.summary: A man betrothed a woman with a bundle of rags. Rav Shimi bar Hiyya, sitting before Rav, examined it to see if it was worth a peruta: if yes she was betrothed, if not she was not.
11.missing: No result of the examination is reported; the incident is a vehicle for a legal distinction.

12.actor: Rabbi Hanina, his wife, and a pauper
12.event: Rabbi Hanina sent his wife with the four dinars he gave a pauper every Shabbat eve.
12.turn: She came back saying the man did not need it, because she heard people in his house asking whether he dined on silver or gold tablecloths.
12.outcome: Rabbi Hanina answered that we should be grateful to swindlers, since without them we would sin daily by not giving to the truly poor.
12.summary: Rabbi Hanina regularly sent a pauper four dinars every Friday afternoon. One day his wife took it and returned saying the man didn't need it, since she heard him being asked whether he ate off silver or gold tablecloths. Rabbi Hanina responded with Rabbi Elazar's saying that we should thank swindlers, for without them we would sin every day.
12.missing: It is not said whether Rabbi Hanina went on giving the money.

13.event: Rabbi Hiyya bar Ashi, who prayed to be saved from the evil inclination, was approached by his wife in disguise as the prostitute Haruta while he studied in his garden.
13.turn: He propositioned her and fetched the pomegranate she demanded; at home he found his wife lighting the oven and sat in it, and she revealed it had been she.
13.outcome: He said he had still intended to transgress, and fasted for the rest of his life until he died.
13.summary: Rabbi Hiyya bar Ashi always prayed to be saved from the evil inclination, and his wife wondered why when he had long since withdrawn from her. One day she dressed up and passed him in his garden, calling herself Haruta. He propositioned her, climbed to get the pomegranate she asked for, and they lay together. At home he sat in the burning oven in shame; she told him it was she, but since he had intended a sin he fasted until he died.

15.event: Rav Rehumi, who studied before Rava, used to come home every Yom Kippur eve but one year got caught up in his study.
15.turn: His wife waited, saying now he is coming, and a tear fell from her eye when he did not come.
15.outcome: At that moment the roof he was sitting on collapsed and he died.
15.summary: Rav Rehumi studied away from home and came back each Yom Kippur eve. One year he was absorbed in a halakha and did not come, while his wife kept waiting and finally shed a tear. At that very moment the roof he was sitting on gave way beneath him and he died.

16.event: Rabbi Hiyya bar Ami's slave immersed a gentile woman for the sake of relations, and Rav Yosef said he could render her and her daughter fit.
16.summary: Rabbi Hiyya bar Ami's slave immersed a gentile woman, intending only to permit relations. Rav Yosef declared that he could treat both her and her daughter as fit to marry into Israel.
16.missing: It is a case plus a ruling; no consequences or ending are told.

17.event: Rabban Gamliel's daughter was married to his brother Abba, who died childless, and Rabban Gamliel entered levirate marriage with her rival wife.
17.outcome: The Gemara then rejects the incident as a proof because she was an aylonit.
17.summary: Rabban Gamliel's daughter was married to his brother Abba, who died without children. Rabban Gamliel then took Abba's other wife in levirate marriage. The Gemara questions whether this proves anything, since Rabban Gamliel followed Beit Hillel.
17.missing: It is cited as legal evidence in one sentence, with no development.

18.event: A brewer betrothed a woman with sediment from beer he was making for someone else.
18.turn: The owner found him and said why not give her from the sharper sediment, and the brewer asked Rava whether this meant the owner had relinquished it.
18.outcome: Rava ruled the owner spoke only out of embarrassment, so the sediment was not given up and she was not betrothed.
18.summary: A brewer making date beer for another man betrothed a woman using sediment from it. The owner came upon him and said he should have used the sharper sediment instead. The brewer asked Rava whether that meant the owner had agreed, and Rava answered that the owner spoke only out of embarrassment, so the woman was not betrothed.

19.event: While Rabbi Yehuda and others sat before Rabbi Tarfon, a yevama came to perform halitza.
19.turn: Rabbi Tarfon told everyone to answer three times 'He who had his shoe removed'.
19.summary: Rabbi Yehuda recalled sitting with others before Rabbi Tarfon when a yevama came to perform halitza. Rabbi Tarfon told them all to respond three times, 'He who had his shoe removed.'
19.missing: It is a short recollection serving as a legal precedent, with no turn or ending.

20.actor: Rav Pappa and Rav Huna son of Rav Yehoshua
20.event: Yeimar bar Hashu's agent seized a boat left by a dead debtor, and Rav Pappa and Rav Huna told him he cannot seize assets to the harm of other creditors.
20.turn: Being creditors themselves, the two seized the boat, each declaring he had acquired all of it, and Rav PineHas bar Ami challenged them.
20.outcome: They came before Rava, who called them white geese who strip people of their cloaks and ruled it did not count because the boat was seized after the debtor died.
20.summary: Yeimar bar Hashu sent his agent to seize a boat the dead debtor left behind. Rav Pappa and Rav Huna rebuked him for harming other creditors, then seized the boat themselves, one steering with an oar and the other pulling with a rope, each claiming all of it. When challenged, they took the case to Rava, who scolded them as white geese who take people's cloaks and ruled that seizure must occur while the debtor is alive.
